transcript:
Meeting header
Date/Time: 2027-01-09 16:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Sasha Kim (Redwood AE), Miguel Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Chen (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Helix Head of ML), Tom Beck (Infra), Angela Li (CTO), Ravi Patel (ML eng)

Summary (auto): Focus on latency and throughput: p95 targets, concurrency, streaming behaviour, and benchmarking methodology.

Transcript:
[00:00] Sasha: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Sasha Kim from Redwood, AE on the account. Quick round robin?
[00:06] Priya R: Hi, Priya Rao here. I'm Head of ML at Helix Payments. We run a mix of hosted APIs and some in-house microservices. Looking at Redwood for predictable inference during transaction spikes.
[00:18] Tom: Tom Beck, infra. I'll be focused on networking and peering.
[00:22] Angela: Angela Li, CTO. I'm here for high-level constraints and compliance.
[00:26] Miguel: Miguel Alvarez, solutions engineer at Redwood, I'll take the performance bits.
[00:30] Sasha: Great. High level - why now? Priya?
[00:34] Priya R: We're seeing higher rates for fraud-detection scoring, context windows are small - 50 to 120 tokens - but p95s matter a lot because these decisions block transactions. Our internal SLO is p95 < 250ms for short prompts. At peak we see bursts up to ~2000 concurrent requests for scoring, which maps to about 3000 to 4000 tokens/sec aggregate depending on model.
[00:56] Miguel: Okay, that's helpful. Are you streaming responses back to your frontends or are they blocking?
[01:00] Priya R: Mostly blocking - we need the final label - but for some enrichment we stream partial results. Streaming stability is a concern; we've seen connection resets with current provider during spikes.
[01:12] Sasha: And current providers? You said hosted OpenAI and internal?
[01:16] Priya R: Yes. We use OpenAI for most non-sensitive flows and our in-house model for PCI-scoped scoring. But costs are high and our internal stack isn't as reliable under bursts.
[01:26] Miguel: Two threads we'll need to cover: 1) latency SLOs for p95 under your concurrency profile and 2) how streaming and batching will affect latency. Also private deployment options if you need VPC/on-prem for PCI.
[01:40] Angela: On PCI, we need KMS integration, audit logs retained for 7 years, SOC2 level controls. How mature is Redwood's private offering?
[01:49] Sasha: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM and audit logging. We have templates for SOC2 controls; I can send the SOC2 package. Miguel, correct me if I misstate.
[01:58] Miguel: That's right. For private we support SAML/SSO, RBAC and KMS. Audit logs are shipped to your storage bucket; retention policy configurable. For latency, one thing to consider is model selection and quantization - smaller models and int8 can significantly reduce p95. But quantization sometimes affects quality for edge cases.
[02:16] Ravi: Quick question: when you say p95 < 250ms, is that for generation-only or end-to-end including network?
[02:22] Miguel: Good call - p95 is server-side inference time. Add your network RTT; with VPC peering we can usually keep the round-trip to under 10-20ms inside the region.
[02:30] Tom: Our peering windows are fine, but in PCI we need egress controls. We'll need details about private control plane vs data plane.
[02:38] Sasha: We'll include an architecture note: control plane can be hosted while data plane sits in your VPC for private deployments.
[02:44] Priya R: Benchmarking: we want token/sec and per-request p95 for sequences 32, 64, 128 tokens. Also concurrency scaling - how p95 shifts as concurrency goes from 50 -> 500 -> 2000.
[02:56] Miguel: Perfect. Our perf-run typically runs three seq lengths, and uses a mix of batching profiles. For example, a dedicated pool with continuous batching gives better throughput but single-request p95 can vary depending on batch wait time cap. For low latency SLOs we set max batch delay to 3-5ms and size caps.
[03:12] Angela: In practice, does the dedicated pool guarantee p95?
[03:16] Miguel: Dedicated capacity gives predictable throughput and a much tighter p95 distribution because you're not competing with noisy neighbors. We also expose autoscaling policies and burst capacity. For hard SLOs under 250ms we often recommend dedicated with a conservative buffer.
[03:29] Priya R: What's the token/sec per GPU ballpark for your recommended models?
[03:33] Miguel: Depends on model and quantization. Example: a 7B int8 variant on A100-class hardware can do roughly 600-1200 tokens/sec depending on sequence length and batching; a 13B might be 300-600 tokens/sec. For strict p95 under 250ms on short prompts we often use 7B+ distils or optimized kernels.
[03:50] Ravi: Do you have streaming performance numbers? We need stable half-open streams for partial enrichments.
[03:55] Miguel: We stream fine. The key is connection management - we support HTTP/2 and chunked responses; for spikes we recommend sticky routing or connection pools to avoid resets. We've seen resets with other providers when autoscaling triggers. Our runtime does graceful fallback to lower-capacity model variants to keep streams alive.
[04:13] Tom: What about batching - can batching hurt p95 for low-latency prompts?
[04:17] Miguel: Yes - batching increases throughput but adds queuing latency. We tune batch wait time and have continuous batching with latency caps. You can set policy per route: e.g., critical scoring route -> no batching, reserved concurrency; enrichment route -> batching on.
[04:31] Priya R: For our workloads, the scoring route is most critical. Enrichment can be async. So we care about concurrency = 2000 burst, baseline 200 RPS, p95 < 250ms. Is that feasible on hosted?
[04:44] Sasha: Hosted can be used for non-PCI flows, but for that tight p95 under heavy burst we usually recommend Dedicated. Hosted can work if you're comfortable with variable performance and fallback strategies.
[04:54] Miguel: Also, caching helps if inputs repeat. Prefix/KV caching can reduce repeated computation and improves p95 for repeated contexts.
[05:02] Priya R: We do have repeating patterns in prompts for certain merchant checks. Would love more detail on caching behavior.
[05:08] Miguel: We'll include caching guide. It covers prefix caching, shard considerations, and how it behaves across Dedicated pools.
[05:15] Angela: Security again - who holds encryption keys for private?
[05:18] Miguel: Customer holds KMS keys in private deployments; Redwood can integrate with your KMS or HSM. For hosted, we offer managed keys but for PCI you should choose private so you control keys.
[05:28] Ravi: On SLOs, do you publish p95 dashboards per route?
[05:31] Sasha: Yes - Redwood Console has per-route p95, token billing, and traces. We'll give you a demo in the deep-dive.
[05:38] Tom: Network egress and NAT - we need to know IP ranges for allow-listing if hosted is used for non-PCI.
[05:44] Sasha: We'll send IP ranges and peering docs.
[05:48] Miguel: For benchmarking, we'll propose a perf-run with reproducible configs: model name & revision, sequence lengths (32/64/128), concurrency sweep (50/200/500/1000/2000), and both streaming and blocking modes. We'll gather p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec.
[06:05] Priya R: That sounds good. How long does a perf-run take?
[06:09] Miguel: End-to-end, 2-4 hours for a thorough sweep per model on Dedicated infra, but scheduling and analysis usually spans 1-2 days. We can run a lighter smoke test in an hour.
[06:18] Angela: Cost question - what's order magnitude difference between hosted and dedicated?
[06:22] Sasha: Hosted is pay-as-you-go per token; Dedicated is reserved capacity with monthly commit. For sustained large throughput, Dedicated saves substantially. We'll include sample math for your prompts once we have prompt corpus.
[06:34] Priya R: Ok, next steps?
[06:36] Sasha: We'll do: Redwood shares pricing and perf-run plan, Helix sends prompt set and infra diagram. Schedule a 90-min deep technical session with your infra and security folks.
[06:46] Tom: I'll coordinate the peering window and security contact.
[06:49] Angela: Please include SOC2 materials and KMS integration doc.
[06:53] Sasha: Yep. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the docs and proposed times.
[06:58] Priya R: Thanks.
[07:00] Meeting ends.

Notes and imperfections: Some names got swapped in auto-transcript (Priya Chen vs Priya Rao), minor words like "KV cash" for KV cache, "Dedicate" for Dedicated in one auto note. These reflect typical Fireflies transcription errors.
